paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Lyle took place in Smyth County, Virginia, in February 1882, after James N. Mercer was shot dead near Town House in a quarrel with Lyle and his brother over Mercer's canoe. According to a Lynchburg dispatch, the sheriff rescued Lyle just as a mob was about to hang him from a tree, while the Bristol News said local citizens were restrained with difficulty from lynching both brothers after they were jailed at Marion. Lyle was convicted of second-degree murder in late April and sentenced to eighteen years in the penitentiary. None of the reports stated the race of anyone involved.

James Mercer, described by the Bristol News as a highly respected citizen "of considerable means" and a blacksmith by trade, lived on the bank of the Middle Fork of the Holston River opposite Town House. He kept a canoe for crossing the river and for other private purposes. The News added that he was a Mason, about 50 years old, and left a wife and several children, some of them married.

On Saturday afternoon, February 18, two young brothers named Lyle took the canoe without permission, crossed the river and left the boat some distance below the regular landing, according to the Bristol News. When Mercer called out that he would put them over, they answered with cursing and abuse. Mercer then rode across behind a passing citizen and asked why they had treated him so, whereupon one brother took out a pistol and handed it to the other, who shot Mercer through the heart. Mercer lived a little over an hour.

The Lynchburg special telegram to the Richmond Dispatch gave a shorter version, saying the quarrel arose because the Lyle brothers had taken "forcible possession" of Mercer's boat. In that account the man who fired was captured and "barely escaped lynching," the sheriff rescuing him as the mob was swinging him to a tree. The Bristol News instead reported that both brothers were arrested at once and lodged in the jail at Marion, and that "the citizens of the vicinity" were kept from lynching them only with difficulty.

Mercer was buried with Masonic rites on the Sunday after the shooting. On Thursday, April 27, Thomas Lyle was found guilty of murder in the second degree and sentenced to eighteen years' confinement in the penitentiary, the Richmond Dispatch reported. He was received at the penitentiary on May 6 along with two other convicts from Smyth County, and the Bristol News noted his sentence on May 9. No report of action against the would-be lynchers, or of what became of the second brother, was found in the coverage.

A brief Lynchburg wire called Mercer "prominent" or "highly-respected" and said the killer "barely escaped lynching." The Richmond Dispatch ran the fuller special telegram under the heading "Fatal Shooting and a Narrow Escape from Lynching in Smyth County," and the Alexandria Gazette printed the same text among its Virginia news. The shorter wire ran on February 21 and 22 in the Savannah Morning News, in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer under the column head "The Trail of Blood," in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, and in the Dallas Daily Herald, which placed the killing in "Smith county." The Washington Evening Star reported the shooting in one sentence and left out the lynching attempt.

The Bristol News, the nearest paper to the scene, called the killing "a most foul and unprovoked murder" and described both Lyles as "bad characters." No paper stated the race of Mercer, the Lyles or the crowd.

On the lynching attempt, the Lynchburg telegram said the sheriff saved the captured man as he was being swung to a tree, while the Bristol News, a local paper with the fuller account, placed the threat after both brothers were in the Marion jail and said only that the citizens were restrained. The reports also differ on the date and on how many men were threatened: the News put the shooting on Saturday afternoon and spoke of both brothers, while the Alexandria Gazette and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said "yesterday" and the wire named one man, Lyle.

framing.detail: Richmond Dispatch heading 'Fatal Shooting and a Narrow Escape from Lynching in Smyth County'; it reports the rescue without comment on the mob.
Bristol News condemns the killing as 'a most foul and unprovoked murder' and calls the Lyles 'bad characters', but reports the attempt to lynch them without comment.
Savannah and Lancaster papers ran the short Lynchburg wire; Lancaster put it under 'The Trail of Blood'.

versions.value: Captured man rescued by the sheriff as the mob was about to swing him to a tree
Both brothers jailed at Marion; citizens restrained with difficulty from lynching them

conflicts.note: The Bristol News is local and fuller on the shooting; the Lynchburg telegram is a separate source with a more dramatic version of the lynching attempt. Neither is clearly better on that point.
The local weekly's 'last Saturday', with burial on Sunday, is the more specific; the wire 'yesterday' may refer to when the news arrived.
The wire's sheriff-rescue story concerns 'him'; the Bristol News speaks of lynching 'them'. Only Thomas Lyle appears in the trial reports.
The original page OCR reads '30'; the re-read text and his married children point to 50.
